articles.title: Amazon Bedrock AgentCore: How AWS Built Multi-Agent Orchestration for Engineering Decision Workflows
articles.excerpt: AWS just published the first detailed look at AgentCore, their multi-agent orchestration layer inside Amazon Bedrock. The use case is aerospace component substitution: an engineer needs to evaluate wh…
articles.body: AWS just published the first detailed look at AgentCore, their multi-agent orchestration layer inside Amazon Bedrock. The use case is aerospace component substitution: an engineer needs to evaluate whether part B can replace part A in a certified aircraft system. Traditionally this takes days of manual cross-referencing across PDFs, CAD drawings, spec sheets, and regulatory documents. AWS compressed it to minutes by coordinating specialized agents that gather evidence, validate compliance, and surface recommendations while keeping the human engineer as the final decision-maker. This is not a demo. The architecture reveals production patterns for state flow between agents, human-in-the-loop approval gates, multimodal evidence retrieval, and failure handling in managed cloud infrastructure.

articles.title: GitHub Octoverse 2026: What 7.38 Billion Monthly Commits Reveal About Agent-Generated Code Infrastructure
articles.excerpt: GitHub's Octoverse 2026 report shows merged pull requests tripled to 220 million per month in less than a year. Commits more than tripled to 7.38 billion per month, with most growth in H2 2026. New re…
articles.body: GitHub's Octoverse 2026 report shows merged pull requests tripled to 220 million per month in less than a year. Commits more than tripled to 7.38 billion per month, with most growth in H2 2026. New repository creation doubled to 30.3 million per month. These numbers represent the first platform-scale measurement of agentic engineering impact, and the methodology behind them exposes interesting infrastructure choices for measuring agent activity at scale. The report introduces LLM-based classification for both repository taxonomy and geolocation correction. GitHub used a fine-tuned multilingual embedding model to sort repositories into NAICS sectors and applied LLM classification to extract country codes from user profiles to correct VPN bias. This is not just measurement.

articles.body: Journey Before Destination I got into software engineering because I enjoyed it. I enjoyed the process of learning, the feeling of writing something and knowing that those sets of instructions were successful in achieving whatever goal they were set out to achieve, and that they did exactly what was needed. Sometimes, things did what was needed but not in the way you expected. For many of us, it didn't matter how something worked as long as it worked. For a crazy few of us, however, it did. So we set out to figure out why something worked when we expected it not to, and then, being the crazy folks we were, we wanted to change that working code and break it. That sounds quite ridiculous if the thing being made wasn't software but some sort of physical object.

articles.title: What I Learned Evaluating AI Image, Video and Audio Models
articles.excerpt: Part of my week is spent as a freelance AI evaluator. I review output from AI models that generate images, video, audio and user interfaces, and score each one against a structured rubric. It is detai…
articles.body: Part of my week is spent as a freelance AI evaluator. I review output from AI models that generate images, video, audio and user interfaces, and score each one against a structured rubric. It is detailed work, and it has changed how I think about building software. The first lesson: following instructions matters more than looking good. An image can be beautiful, but if the prompt asked for three people and the model drew four, it failed the task. A plainer result that does exactly what was asked is the better answer. That rule applies to almost everything I build now. Do what the user asked first, then make it pretty. The second lesson: false positives are worse than misses. When you flag a problem that is not really there, you send the people training the model in the wrong direction.

articles.title: NASA's Swift space telescope crashes back to Earth after failed rescue attempt
articles.excerpt: NASA's Swift space telescope crashed back to Earth today (Nov. 4), three months after a private spacecraft was supposed to boost the observatory to a higher orbit.
articles.body: NASA's Swift space telescope has reached the end of its long and winding road. Swift fell uncontrolled to Earth today (Nov. 4), 22 years after it launched but just three months after a private spacecraft was supposed to boost it to a higher, life-extending orbit. The 3,200-pound (1,450 kilograms) observatory reentered Earth's atmosphere at 7:39 a.m. EST (1239 GMT) today over northern Sumatra, according to satellite tracker Jonathan McDowell , who cited U.S. Space Force data. The fall likely didn't make much of an impact; NASA officials predicted beforehand that most of the minibus-sized Swift would burn up as it fell, and they put the odds of any of the surviving pieces hurting anyone on Earth at just 1 in 2,100.

articles.title: Mars isn't dead — recent volcanic activity reveals it's just sleeping
articles.excerpt: Scientists have long suspected that Mars is geologically "dead" but new spacecraft observations suggests the Red Planet's volcanoes are merely sleeping.
articles.body: Scientists have long suspected that Mars is geologically "dead," but new spacecraft observations suggest the Red Planet's volcanoes are merely sleeping. That means that Olympus Mons , the extinct Martian volcano that at around 16 miles (26 kilometers) above the surrounding Martian plains is the largest mountain in the solar system , may in fact be a slumbering giant. The observations were made with the European Space Agency (ESA) mission ExoMars Trace Gas Orbiter (TGO) as it studied volcanic fissures along the Alba Mons region of the Red Planet. Alba Mons is in the Tharsis region of Mars, the same area that is home to Olympus Mons.

articles.title: NASA's Artemis II moon launch tore a hole in Earth's upper atmosphere so huge it disrupted GPS signals
articles.excerpt: "It could have a strong impact not only on self-driving cars but also on drone positioning."
articles.body: The launch of NASA's Artemis II mission in April 2026 caused significant disturbances in Earth's ionosphere that could have triggered temporary, localized errors in GPS positioning, a new study has found. The study, by a team of researchers from National Cheng Kung University in Taiwan, analyzed data from high-precision networks of fixed, ground-based GPS receivers, used by U.S. scientific institutions to measure the minuscule motions of Earth's tectonic plates in the lead-up to earthquakes.

articles.title: NASA Navigation Experiment Shows Promise for Planetary Landings
articles.excerpt: NASA successfully demonstrated technology designed to help spacecraft autonomously navigate to safe landing sites on the Moon and on other planets. An Alta-X drone equipped with the agency’s Safe and…
articles.body: 3 min read Preparations for Next Moonwalk Simulations Underway (and Underwater) An Alta-X drone flies an advanced guidance and navigation system known as the Safe and Precise Landing – Integrated Capabilities Evolution (SPLICE) experiment near NASA’s Armstrong Flight Research Center in Edwards, California, on Wednesday, July 15, 2026. Researchers at NASA’s Johnson Space Center in Houston developed SPLICE, which successfully communicated with the remotely piloted aircraft during hover maneuvers in flight. SPLICE will help spacecraft land precisely and detect and avoid potential hazards, which is critical for NASA missions to the Moon and to Mars.
